claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9001
claims.text: Sec. 9001 of Division G, S. 2226 as engrossed in the Senate: 'This division may be cited as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023" or the "UAP Disclosure Act of 2023".'

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9010(a)-(b)
claims.text: EMINENT DOMAIN PROVISION, verbatim. Sec. 9010(a): 'Exercise of Eminent Domain.--The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Sec. 9010(b): 'Any and all such material, should it exist, shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material and in a timely manner conducive to the objectives of the Review Board in accordance with the requirements of this division.'

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9010(c)
claims.text: Sec. 9010(c) directs the Review Board to render decisions '(1) whether the material examined constitutes technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence beyond a reasonable doubt; (2) whether recovered technologies of unknown origin, biological evidence of non-human intelligence, or a particular subset of material qualifies for postponement of disclosure under this division; and (3) what changes, if any, to the current disposition of said material should the Federal Government make to facilitate full disclosure.'

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9010(d)-(e)
claims.text: Sec. 9010(d)-(e): the Review Board 'shall have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession' and 'shall solicit additional unidentified anomalous phenomena witness and whistleblower testimony and afford protections under section 1673(b) of the James M. Inhofe National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2023 (50 U.S.C. 3373b(b))'. The phrase 'legacy program personnel' is statutory text in the Senate-passed bill.

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9007(a)-(b)
claims.text: REVIEW BOARD PROVISION, verbatim. Sec. 9007(a): 'Establishment.--There is established as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board".' Sec. 9007(b)(1): 'The President, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, shall appoint, without regard to political affiliation, 9 citizens of the United States to serve as members of the Review Board to ensure and facilitate the review, transmission to the Archivist, and public disclosure of government records relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena.'

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9007(b)(4)(A)
claims.text: Sec. 9007(b)(4)(A) disqualifies nominees who 'shall be impartial citizens, none of whom shall have had any previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence' - the bill text presupposes such programs and controlling authorities exist.

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9007(b)(3)-(4)
claims.text: Sec. 9007(b)(3)(A) requires the President to consider nominees recommended by the Senate majority and minority leaders, the Speaker and House minority leader, the Secretary of Defense, the National Academy of Sciences, 'Established nonprofit research organizations relating to unidentified anomalous phenomena', and the American Historical Association. Board composition under 9007(b)(4)(C) must include at least 1 current or former national security official, 1 current or former foreign service official, 1 scientist or engineer, 1 economist, 1 professional historian, and 1 sociologist.

claims.source: S.2226 engrossed in Senate, BILLS-118s2226es, Div. G sec. 9002(a)(4)
claims.text: Congressional findings enacted in the Senate text, sec. 9002(a)(4): 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ..., as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.'

sources.name: S. 2226 (Engrossed in Senate) — GPO

desc: The UAP Disclosure Act of 2023 is the only text ever passed by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the assumption that recovered non-human technology and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held, in part, by private entities. It began as S.Amdt. 797, submitted by Senator Schumer on 13 July 2023 for himself and Senators Rounds, Rubio, Gillibrand, Young and Heinrich, and printed in the Congressional Record at 169 Cong. Rec. S2953-S2959. It travelled into the engrossed Senate bill as Division G, Sections 9001 through 9015, and the Senate passed it on 27 July 2023. Section 9002 states the premise in statutory findings: that legislation is necessary 'because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified,' in part because of Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an 'over-broad interpretation of transclassified foreign nuclear information.' Section 9003 defines 'non-human intelligence' as 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin,' defines 'legacy program' to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment, and defines 'controlling authority' to include any private entity in physical possession of such material. Sections 9004 through 9006 create a Records Collection at the National Archives with a presumption of immediate disclosure. Sections 9007 through 9009 create a nine-member Review Board appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, barred from including anyone with previous or current involvement in any legacy program, empowered to order disclosure absent clear and convincing evidence for postponement, and required to produce a Controlled Disclosure Campaign Plan. Section 9010 orders the exercise of eminent domain. Section 9014 authorises $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024. Sections 9007 through 9011 and 9014 were removed in conference and have never been enacted.

claims.text: The provisions removed in conference are exactly the ones that would have moved custody out of the hands of current holders or compelled testimony from legacy-program personnel; the provisions that survived are the ones administered by the same original classification authorities that hold the records.

dossier.denialPosture: No executive branch office has ever publicly explained why the Review Board and eminent domain sections were removed in conference, and no conference report language identifying an objecting party has been made public. The Department of Defense has never responded on the record to the bill's finding that Atomic Energy Act exemptions and transclassified foreign nuclear information are being used to keep UAP records out of mandatory declassification review.
dossier.narrative:
On 13 July 2023 the Senate Majority Leader rose and submitted an amendment to the defence bill. The Congressional Record entry is flat and procedural - 'SA 797. Mr. SCHUMER (for himself, Mr. Rounds, Mr. Rubio, Mrs. Gillibrand, Mr. Young, and Mr. Heinrich) submitted an amendment intended to be proposed by him to the bill S. 2226 ... which was ordered to lie on the table' - and what follows across seven pages of the Record is the most consequential UAP text in American law.

The structure is deliberately modelled on the President John F. Kennedy Assassination Records Collection Act of 1992: a records collection at the National Archives, a presumption of immediate disclosure, an independent review board with the power to override agency postponement, and a sunset. The differences are where the argument lives. The JFK Act dealt only with paper. This bill deals with objects.

The findings section states the premise. Congress finds that 'Legislation is necessary because credible evidence and testimony indicates that Federal Government unidentified anomalous phenomena records exist that have not been declassified or subject to mandatory declassification review as set forth in Executive Order 13526 ... due in part to exemptions under the Atomic Energy Act of 1954 ..., as well as an over-broad interpretation of "transclassified foreign nuclear information", which is also exempt from mandatory declassification, thereby preventing public disclosure under existing provisions of law.' That is a named legal mechanism of concealment, identified by the Senate, and it points at the Department of Energy and the Restricted Data regime rather than at the Department of Defense alone. The next finding says the Freedom of Information Act 'has proven inadequate.'

The definitions do the load-bearing work. 'Controlling authority' means 'any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.' A commercial company cannot be in physical possession of a thing that does not exist. 'Legacy program' is defined to include 'commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.' 'Non-human intelligence' means 'any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.'

The Review Board provisions establish 'as an independent agency a board to be known as the "Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Review Board"', appointed by the President with the advice and consent of the Senate, nine citizens, without regard to political affiliation. Board staff must be citizens 'of integrity and impartiality who ha[ve] had no previous or current involvement with any legacy program or controlling authority relating to the collection, exploitation, or reverse engineering of technologies of unknown origin or the examination of biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence.' A statute does not write a conflict-of-interest bar against a category of person that Congress believes to be empty.

Then the section that made the bill unpassable. 'The Federal Government shall exercise eminent domain over any and all recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence that may be controlled by private persons or entities in the interests of the public good.' Such material 'shall be made available to the Review Board for personal examination and subsequent disclosure determination at a location suitable to the controlling authority of said material.' The Board would then decide whether the material constitutes technologies of unknown origin 'beyond a reasonable doubt', whether it qualifies for postponement, and 'what changes, if any, to the current disposition of said material should the Federal Government make to facilitate full disclosure.' The Board would also 'have access to all testimony from unidentified anomalous phenomena witnesses, close observers and legacy program personnel and whistleblowers within the Federal Government's possession.'

The money section authorised $20,000,000 for fiscal year 2024 and, pending appropriation, permitted the President to use 'such sums as are available for discretionary use.'

What was enacted on 22 December 2023 in Public Law 118-31 is three sections - 1841, 1842 and 1843 - creating the Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Records Collection at the National Archives, requiring agencies to review, identify, transmit and disclose UAP records, and setting out grounds for postponement. There is no Review Board. There is no eminent domain. There is no authorisation of appropriations. There is no witness-solicitation mandate. The surviving regime asks the original classification authorities that hold the records to identify their own records and to invoke their own postponement grounds, and gives no independent body the power to say no.

That is the argument. The Senate wrote a bill whose operative theory was that the material is held by controlling authorities including private companies, that those companies will not surrender it voluntarily, and that only compulsory acquisition plus an outside board with special access clearances could break the hold. Conference removed compulsion and removed the outside board. What remains is a filing cabinet with the same locks and the same keyholders.
openQuestions: Which members or agencies asked for the Review Board and eminent domain sections to be struck in the FY2024 NDAA conference, and in what written form was the request made?
Did any executive branch agency submit a Statement of Administration Policy or legislative-referral objection to Division G, and is it retrievable?
Has any agency ever identified a specific record withheld under the 'transclassified foreign nuclear information' exemption that would otherwise be a UAP record?

The Senate text presupposes controlling authorities in physical possession; no controlling authority has ever been named in any public congressional document. Which entities did the drafters have in mind?

Section numbering differs between the Congressional Record print of SA 797 (SEC. __01 through __15) and the engrossed division; the engrossed section numbers used elsewhere on this board should be re-verified against BILLS-118s2226es directly.

The negative claim that no Review Board or eminent domain text survives in Public Law 118-31 was established here by comparison against NARA's description of the enacted sections rather than by a direct full-text search of the enrolled bill, which should be run to close the point.
dossier.whatItIs: The Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena Disclosure Act of 2023 was submitted by Senator Charles Schumer on 13 July 2023 as Senate Amendment 797 to S. 2226, the FY2024 National Defense Authorization Act, and printed in full in the Congressional Record at pages S2953-S2959. It travelled into the Senate-engrossed NDAA as a freestanding division of fifteen sections. Its enforcement machinery - an independent nine-member Records Review Board, a federal exercise of eminent domain over privately held recovered materials, and a $20,000,000 authorisation - was removed before enactment, leaving only an archiving and postponement regime at sections 1841-1843 of Public Law 118-31.
dossier.whyImplicated: This is the only text ever adopted by a chamber of the United States Congress that legislates on the express premise that recovered technologies of unknown origin and biological evidence of non-human intelligence exist and are held in part by private entities. Its definitions are not rhetorical: 'controlling authority' is defined to include any commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of such material, and 'legacy program' is defined to reach commercial, academic and private-sector reverse-engineering endeavours predating enactment. Six senators including the Majority Leader and the Vice Chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee put their names to a finding that records exist which have been shielded from mandatory declassification review by Atomic Energy Act exemptions and an over-broad reading of transclassified foreign nuclear information. The bill then directs the Federal Government to seize that material by eminent domain and hand it to a board explicitly barred from containing anyone who has ever worked on a legacy program. The provisions that would have moved custody, compelled testimony and paid for the effort are precisely the provisions that did not survive conference - which is the single most informative fact on this node.

entityInfo.desc:
Key statutory definitions as passed by the Senate (Sec. 9003):

(5) 'controlling authority' means any Federal, State, or local government department, office, agency, committee, commission, commercial company, academic institution, or private sector entity in physical possession of technologies of unknown origin or biological evidence of non-human intelligence.

(11) 'legacy program' means all Federal, State, and local government, commercial industry, academic, and private sector endeavors to collect, exploit, or reverse engineer technologies of unknown origin or examine biological evidence of living or deceased non-human intelligence that pre-dates the date of the enactment of this Act.

(13) 'non-human intelligence' means any sentient intelligent non-human lifeform regardless of nature or ultimate origin that may be presumed responsible for unidentified anomalous phenomena or of which the Federal Government has become aware.

(2) 'close observer' means anyone who has come into close proximity to unidentified anomalous phenomena or non-human intelligence.

The Sec. 9003(23) definition of a 'unidentified anomalous phenomena record' reaches twenty-four categories of holder, expressly including the Department of Defense 'and its progenitors, the Department of War and the Department of the Navy'; the Air Force Office of Special Investigations by name; the Department of Energy 'and its progenitors, the Manhattan Project, the Atomic Energy Commission, and the Energy Research and Development Administration'; the CIA 'and its progenitor, the Office of Strategic Services'; the NRO, DIA, NSA, NGA, NASA, FBI, FAA, NOAA and the Library of Congress; and, at subparagraph (X), 'any private sector person or entity formerly or currently under contract or some other agreement with the Federal Government.'
